title: Causally Robust Preference Learning with Reasons
one_liner: ReCouPLe uses the user's stated reason for a preference to train the reward model on the causal feature that matters, instead of letting it rely on spurious context.
lead: Preference-based reward learning usually gets only binary supervision: trajectory A is preferred to trajectory B. That signal is sparse. It tells the model which option won, but not why it won. As a result, the reward model often picks up shortcuts. If safer trajectories in training also happened to be slower, the model may learn to reward slowness rather than safety. ReCouPLe adds the missing reason. It takes a natural-language rationale such as 'avoids collisions with a fragile object' and uses it to define the direction in representation space that should matter for scoring. The point is not to attach extra text for decoration. The point is to isolate the causal feature the user cared about and suppress unrelated context that merely co-occurred during training.

problem.h2: Why binary preferences are easy to misread
paras: A reward model sees paired trajectories and a preference label. If one trajectory wins, standard training tells the model to increase its score. But a trajectory contains many features at once: speed, distance to obstacles, path smoothness, object type, and background context. The label alone does not identify which of those features caused the preference.

That ambiguity creates causal confusion. During training, a preferred property may co-occur with irrelevant properties. A model trained only on winner-versus-loser labels can assign credit to the wrong feature. It will still fit the training data, but it will fail when the spurious correlation disappears or reverses. A reward model that mistakes slowness for safety is one example.

callout.html: Add the stated reason for the preference and force the reward model to score trajectories using the feature direction aligned with that reason.

steps.text: Each preferred trajectory is paired with a short textual reason that states what property justified the choice.
The model maps both trajectories and rationales into a shared representation space so they can be compared directly.

steps.b: Use the rationale as a projection axis
steps.text: Trajectory features aligned with the reason are emphasized, while orthogonal context is de-emphasized.

steps.b: Train preference scores with that projection
steps.text: The reward model is optimized to rank the preferred trajectory higher after filtering through the rationale-aligned direction.

steps.b: Reuse the same reason across tasks
steps.text: A rationale that appears in several tasks can transfer the same causal preference without retraining a new language model.

paras: The paper changes what supervises the reward model. Instead of learning only from binary pairwise wins, it learns from pairwise wins plus the explicit reason that should determine the win.
object.object: the supervision signal for reward learning

hidden.h2: The model must identify the causal feature, not just the winning trajectory
hidden.name: reason-aligned causal direction
paras: The hidden quantity is the feature direction that corresponds to the user's reason. For a rationale about avoiding collisions, the model should respond to collision risk and ignore unrelated factors that happened to travel with low collision risk in the training set.

This quantity matters because preference labels alone underdetermine the cause of a choice. Many distinct feature explanations can fit the same pairwise data. The rationale narrows that set by naming the intended causal factor, so the reward model can anchor its score to the right part of the trajectory representation.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark the parts of the signal that determine whether the reward model learns the true reason or a shortcut.

reads.html: The model is trying to lock onto the feature named by the user rather than any other trait that happened to appear in the preferred trajectory.
Each rationale defines a direction in representation space that should govern scoring, so preference learning is guided toward the articulated causal factor and away from unrelated correlates.

mechanism.h2: Why the reason helps remove causal confusion
paras: A binary preference label says only that one trajectory beat another. Without extra structure, the reward model can explain that win using any feature pattern that separates winners from losers in the training set. That is exactly how shortcut learning enters.

ReCouPLe adds structure by encoding the rationale and using it as a projection axis in the shared representation. Projection means the trajectory is scored according to how much of its representation lies in the direction named by the reason. Features orthogonal to that direction contribute less. This works because the reason selects the subspace that should matter, so the model is discouraged from using unrelated background cues even if those cues correlate with winners in the training data.

The transfer benefit comes from semantic reuse. If two tasks both contain the rationale 'avoids collisions with a fragile object,' then the same direction can be used in both places. The reward model does not need to rediscover the causal feature from scratch on the second task, because the textual reason already points to the same axis. That is why the method can generalize across tasks without extra language-model fine-tuning.

stages.s: encode trajectories and rationale in a shared space
project trajectory features onto the rationale direction
score the pair using that filtered feature signal
reward aligned with the stated reason rather than spurious context

math.words: Score a trajectory by taking the component of its representation that lies along the rationale direction. The reward then depends mainly on that aligned component.
symbols: the trajectory representation produced by the encoder
the rationale representation, used as the direction that selects the relevant feature component

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose trajectory A and trajectory B are equally slow, but only A keeps distance from a fragile object.
The rationale is 'avoids collisions with a fragile object.'
If the trajectory encoder gives A a larger component along the rationale direction than B, then A gets the higher reward.
Background brightness does not help unless it also aligns with the rationale direction.
This is why the reason can block shortcut credit assignment when the training set contains irrelevant correlations.

math.note: The score is conditioned on the reason, so the same trajectory can be rated differently under different stated preferences.

bars.h2: Why the extra reason signal matters

charts.title: Preference learning from binary labels only
charts.note: The model can fit training pairs but still rely on the wrong causes because the label does not specify which feature deserved credit.

charts.title: Preference learning with rationales
charts.note: The rationale improves generalization because it anchors the reward to the named cause instead of to whichever context happened to correlate with winners.

items.b: Reasons can be vague or incomplete.
items.html: If the rationale says only 'better behavior,' it does not isolate a usable causal feature, so the projection direction may still leave room for shortcuts because the model has not been told which property should receive credit.

items.b: The encoder may not represent the needed feature well.
items.html: If collision risk or some other key property is not visible in the trajectory representation, aligning with the rationale direction will not recover it.

items.b: Some preferences depend on multiple reasons.
items.html: A single rationale direction may be too simple when a user cares about several interacting factors at once, such as safety, speed, and comfort together.
The method is strongest when reasons are concrete and reusable across tasks, because then the same direction can serve as a stable causal guide in multiple settings.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Construct a small trajectory dataset where the true preference depends on safety, but speed is spuriously correlated with safety in training and anti-correlated at test time. Train one reward model on binary preferences only and another on binary preferences plus rationales. The demo should show whether the rationale-conditioned model keeps preferring safer trajectories after the correlation flips.
demo.closing: The demo must show that the textual reason changes what feature receives credit, not merely that it adds more supervision volume.
